questions.title: Is existence definable?
questions.question: What is being known when existence is said to be immediately intelligible, and what would a noncircular definition require?
questions.framing: A successful real definition explains a thing by prior and better-known constituents. But the proposed definitions of existence appeal to establishment, to an object about which one can make assertions, or to other notions that themselves presuppose something existent. The question is therefore not whether the word “existence” can be explained; it is whether the concept can be *resolved* into a more basic real definition. Ṭūsī also rejects defective proofs of the correct thesis: the conclusion must not be confused with the quality of every argument for it.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī’s precise target
stages.claim: The opening lemmata reject circular definitions, distinguish lexical explanation from real definition, and disallow certain arguments for indefinability. The rejection of an argument does not amount to a rejection of the conclusion.
stages.transition: This is a logical and semantic problem, not yet a doctrine that all existents are one reality.

stages.heading: A faulty demonstration can have a true conclusion
stages.claim: Lāhījī warns that defeating an argument for the simplicity or indefinability of being does not defeat that conclusion. His own conclusion is that existence is simple and lacks constitutive parts.
stages.transition: Distinguish existence as a simple intelligible from a claim that all extramental existents share one simple entity.

stages.heading: Al-Ḥillī identifies the circle
stages.claim: The attempted definition of the existent as what is established already embeds the very idea to be defined. A definition by the possibility of reporting something equally uses a demonstrative reference to something taken as established.
stages.transition: The operative objection is *prior intelligibility*, not a thesis about the independence of quiddity.

stages.heading: A rule for proper definition
stages.claim: Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī states the general requirement that the definiens be clearer than the definiendum. Ibn Taymiyya criticises the alleged necessity of a particular logical method; that broader criticism is registered as a distinct methodological challenge, not treated as support for Ṭūsī’s exact argument.
stages.transition: The transition from existence to other self-evident modalities occurs at Q10.

stages.claim: Read the following passages in their stated source order. Lāhījī’s alternative interpretations precede his objection; Qūshjī’s reported answer precedes his criticism and decisive reply; İSAM separates Iṣfahānī’s base text from Jurjānī’s gloss. Cross-question placement is editorial comparison, not proof that these authors directly replied to one another.

questions.verdict: The defensible result is modest: proposed explanations of the word are possible, but real definitions that contain existence implicitly are circular. Ṭūsī demands an examination of each purported proof. A common concept of being is an additional thesis, considered separately in Q02.
questions.boundary: No proof of the ontological unity of existence, of its numerical simplicity, or of the mental/external distinction follows from indefinability alone.
questions.remaining: Collate al-Ḥillī on the two rejected arguments in Kashf al-murād, al-Iṣfahānī at the opening of Tasdīd, the corresponding Qūshjī objections, and Sunni discussions of taṣawwur.

questions.title: A common concept or graded realities?
questions.question: Is wujūd predicated with one meaning of the Necessary and contingent beings, and what follows for the realities signified?
questions.framing: Three different claims are frequently conflated: the *meaning* of the predicate existence is common; the predicate is applied to things asymmetrically or analogically; and what exists outside the mind is a single reality. The first does not by itself prove the third. Here the issue is how one meaning can apply to the Necessary and the possible without making them members of a univocal species.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī and al-Ḥillī: retain existence while doubting the subject
stages.claim: The common-concept argument starts not from a mystical thesis but from the fact that one remains certain a cause exists even as one revises whether it is necessary or possible, substance or accident. This shows a stable intelligible predication.
stages.transition: This proves semantic commonality at most; it does not prove one numerically identical extra-mental act of existence.

stages.heading: Lāhījī: concept versus individual existents
stages.claim: An objection would ask whether a universal existent must itself be an external existent. Lāhījī says the concept of existence is intellectual, thereby avoiding treating it as an additional common substance.
stages.transition: Keep this question separate from Q03 (the relation of that concept to an individual quiddity) and from Q27–29 (ontological unity).

stages.heading: Qūnawī raises the divine existence problem
stages.claim: Qūnawī asks whether the Necessary is its own existence if existential meaning is shared; he tests the inference between a common predicate and distinct concrete realities.
stages.transition: This is a new problem of divine essential identity, not simply a repetition of common concept.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī on graded/shared predication
stages.claim: Ṭūsī allows a shared general concept predicated in different ways without conceding numerical unity of extra-mental existences. Yazdī’s three-case argument about gradation in what is essential separates varying individual intensity from intrinsic gradation of one defining concept.
stages.transition: The predicate of a derivative may exhibit graded application even when the universal itself has a stable essential meaning; this distinction becomes relevant to Lāhījī’s later Sufi interpretation but does not decide it.

stages.heading: Sunni comparison and logical boundary
stages.claim: Al-Taftāzānī separates semantic univocity, conceptual addition, and divine simplicity; the historical attribution to al-Ashʿarī requires comparison with his own texts.
stages.transition: Question Q03 asks the status of the predicated concept relative to a quiddity.

stages.heading: The gap from common concept to one existence
stages.claim: Lāhījī entertains a Sufi reading where the universal concept of existence is only intellectual while the externally real ground would be absolute existence. This is presented as a possibility to be tested, not a deduction from concept sharing.
stages.transition: The contested bridge premise is carried forward to Q27 and Q29, where Lāhījī’s independent objection must be faced.

questions.verdict: Qūnawī and Ṭūsī are not simply opposing one shared meaning to many unrelated meanings; they disagree about what the shared meaning commits one to metaphysically. The later Jurjānī–Lāhījī discussion (Q27–29) expressly tests whether existence has distinct realities or only determinations. Keeping these layers separate makes the disagreement intelligible.
questions.boundary: Neither the common concept nor analogical predication settles identity of divine existence, gradation of realities, or waḥdat al-wujūd without further premises.

Still required: independent edition/manuscript variants; direct verification of Jurjānī’s reported unity argument and Dawwānī’s adoption; the full original five-stage exchange and Ghiyāth’s response.

questions.title: The addition of existence to quiddity
questions.question: Is existence distinct from essence in intellect, in reality, or as a really inhering accident?
questions.framing: If an essence can be grasped without judging it to exist, existence is not included in that essence’s definition. But what sort of distinction is this? An accidental form inhering in an already existent subject would seem to demand the existence of that subject before existence arrives; a purely verbal distinction would not account for informative existential predication. The central issue is to identify the respect in which existence is said to be “added.”

stages.heading: First: common existence is not the essence of every thing
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī argues: if shared existence were identical to every distinct essence, all essences would collapse into one; if it were an internal generic component, every differentiating feature would also require existence, threatening an infinite complexity.
stages.transition: The entailment concerns conceptual identity/essential composition, not yet an additional physical accident.

stages.heading: Second: quiddity can be known while existence is in doubt
stages.claim: The cognitive proof begins with a determinate understanding of an essence where both mental and external existence remain in question. Distinguish epistemic separation from a mind-independent split into two independently existent things.
stages.transition: This is the point of the regress objection: whether existence itself needs a second existence.

stages.heading: The mind can apprehend quiddity without apprehending its existence
stages.claim: Lāhījī answers the claim that conceiving an essence entails conceiving its mental existence by distinguishing the occurrence of a thought from the content thought about.
stages.transition: Therefore the distinctness argument is demonstrably conceptual, and cannot by itself establish separate extra-mental components.

stages.heading: Third: existential judgments have informative content
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī also argues that we sometimes require evidence for existence; predication and denial would be pointless or contradictory if existence were simply intrinsic to the definition of every quiddity.
stages.transition: The same argument should not be misread to say that nonexistent quiddities are separately established real objects (Q05).

stages.heading: Al-Taftāzānī distinguishes intellectual and extra-mental addition
stages.claim: The regress/dilemma is answered by distinguishing the intellect’s consideration of existence from an actual accident inhering in a previously existent essence.
stages.transition: Potential difference in metaphysical commitments must not be ironed out.

stages.heading: Causing existence does not alter intrinsic quiddity
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī’s causal observation distinguishes making an essence exist from making an essence what it is; this supports the distinction without giving an uncritical Muʿtazilī thingness doctrine.
stages.transition: Next questions Q04–05 turn to quiddity in itself and the status of nonactual things.

questions.verdict: The sources converge on the necessity of distinguishing concept from external instantiation, while differing over how far this distinction goes in the Necessary. The core answer is not “there are two external things, essence and its existence,” but that existential attribution is intellectually informative without being an independently inhering external property.
questions.boundary: The ontology of *distinct external existences* remains contested; the anti-regress distinction alone does not settle it.

questions.title: Quiddity in itself and the three considerations
questions.question: What is meant by māhiyya min ḥaythu hiya, bi-sharṭ lā, and lā bi-sharṭ, and do any imply a freestanding essence?
questions.framing: Quiddity considered “in itself” is neither an actually existing external universal nor a third ontic realm. It is a rule for what belongs to the intelligible content *precisely qua* that content. This allows one to say that humanity as such is not intrinsically characterised by existence or nonexistence, while avoiding the logical absurdity of asserting that a thing lacks both members of a contradiction absolutely.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī distinguishes the considerations
stages.claim: The lemmata distinguish quiddity as itself, quiddity with accompanying restrictions, quiddity with other things excluded, and quiddity without condition. The natural, logical, and intellectual universals must not be collapsed.
stages.transition: The point is primarily about modes of consideration and predication.

stages.heading: Ṭihrānī answers the contradiction objection
stages.claim: Ṭihrānī clarifies that the phrase “in itself” brackets properties extraneous to the quiddity’s definition. He explicitly asks whether denying both contradictories is being allowed, then differentiates absence of inclusion in the essence from absolute negation of a predicate.
stages.transition: This explains why the expression is legitimate without inventing a neutral state between existence and nonexistence.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī replies to Qūnawī’s making question
stages.claim: The correspondence asks whether possible quiddities are made. Ṭūsī distinguishes what belongs to them as abstracted quiddities from their mental and extra-mental existence, each of which has an appropriate account of causation.
stages.transition: This raises the issue of divine intelligibles and possibilities, followed in Q26.

questions.verdict: The doctrine furnishes a logical distinction indispensable for later debates. It does not assert that quiddities have independent existence prior to being caused. The important test is to distinguish not-being-included-in-a-definition from a positive negation of an actual predicate.
questions.boundary: A quiddity’s neutral consideration must not be equated without argument with Muʿtazilī extramental thubūt or Akbarī aʿyān thābita.
questions.remaining: Full primary comparison of Ṭihrānī pp.128–130 with Ḥillī and Qūshjī on the universal; add Ibn Sīnā, al-Rāzī and al-Taftāzānī control passages.

questions.title: Thingness, establishment, and the nonexistent
questions.question: Can a possible-but-nonexistent quiddity be an extramentally established thing, and in which precise sense is this denied?
questions.framing: The dispute over “the nonexistent is a thing” concerns *which kind of establishment* is affirmed, not whether humans can think of something absent. The strong contested position says a possible quiddity has determinate establishment outside the mind without existential actuality. Other positions accept knowability or specificity while denying that external ontic status.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī’s direct denial, interpreted by Iṣfahānī
stages.claim: Iṣfahānī presents the thesis that thingness is coextensive with existence, and narrows the disputed Muʿtazilī claim to possible, not impossible, nonexistent quiddities.
stages.transition: A refutation that merely shows inexistents lack *effects* would not refute the opponent’s more limited conception of thubūt.

stages.heading: Jurjānī challenges an equivocation
stages.claim: Jurjānī distinguishes establishment qua intrinsic determinacy from actual effect-bearing existence. His point is methodological: a criticism must strike the first sense when that is the one asserted by the opponent.
stages.transition: He does not thereby endorse an extra-mental third realm; he blocks an inadequate rejoinder.

stages.heading: Sunni classification
stages.claim: Al-Taftāzānī reports the debate over whether the nonexistent is a thing and whether states constitute a separate category. These questions are not simply settled by the everyday meaningfulness of fictional or future descriptions.
stages.transition: The status of intellectual thingness is next distinguished in Q06.

questions.verdict: Iṣfahānī’s formulation denies external thingness without existence; Jurjānī requires an exact response to what “establishment” means. The real question is whether possibility and determinacy demand a positive extramental correlate. Q26 will revisit divine knowledge of possible things, without assuming the Akbarī doctrine is this Muʿtazilī thesis in new terminology.
questions.boundary: No included passage proves that all Muʿtazilī authors held one identical doctrine; further first-hand Muʿtazilī texts remain necessary.
questions.remaining: Check the entire Iṣfahānī–Jurjānī passage in the İSAM facsimile, including objections after the quoted beginning; compare the Sunni denial of a third ontic state and Muʿtazilī primary texts.

questions.title: Second intelligibles, states, and logical predication
questions.question: Do logical and metaphysical predicates disclose extra-mental constituents, or can they be objectively applicable without extra-mental instances?
questions.framing: “Thingness,” “universality,” “possibility,” and certain relations can truly be predicated without constituting independent extramental forms. But there are two different problems: identifying a second intelligible and deciding whether its objective basis is merely logical, founded in real properties, or the subject of a distinct dispute about states (aḥwāl).

stages.heading: The claim about thingness
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī identifies thingness and similar predicates as second intelligibles attaching to first intelligibles. Their being attributable to things is not the same as an independently subsisting “thingness” existing alongside them.
stages.transition: This is a logical answer to how something may be a thing, not an endorsement of extramental nonexistent essences.

stages.heading: Controversy about ḥāl
stages.claim: Ṭūsī’s lemmata reject states in the relevant sense and the supposed ontic consequences drawn from them. This should be treated as a separate metaphysical hypothesis, not collapsed into every form of conceptual predication.
stages.transition: The debate requires passages from the opponents of the denial, not only Ṭūsī’s rejection.

stages.heading: al-Sayyid al-Sanad’s challenge and Yazdī’s reply about real attribution
stages.claim: The later gloss transmits al-Sayyid al-Sanad’s challenge that co-presence of two existents is insufficient to make a proposition true; Yazdī replies that real attribution requires a relation of qualification without that relation existing as a third independent entity. Speaker attribution is explicitly controlled. The title is contextually probable for Dashtakī in this edition; it is not direct collation of his original gloss.
stages.transition: This permits a contrast between what grounds an affirmative statement and what is separately present in the world. Neither answer establishes an independent “state” between existence and nonexistence.

questions.verdict: The historical core is the move from conceptual predicability to, or away from, ontic multiplication. A correct argument must establish why a predicate demands a distinct external bearer; merely employing the predicate is insufficient. The polemic about aḥwāl is not therefore a quarrel about whether predicates have meanings.
questions.boundary: No general doctrine of “all second intelligibles are merely subjective” follows: their objective grounding must be considered case by case.

questions.title: Mental existence and the known object
questions.question: When a subject knows heat or a horse, is the quiddity or a cognitive form present, and which properties are thereby predicated?
questions.framing: When I know fire, my mind does not burn. Yet the thought of fire is genuinely an occurrence in my mind and can make “fire is hot” intelligible. The puzzle is to separate the object represented, the intentional content, and the particular psychic act of representing it. Treating them as one item generates false contradictions between substance and accident, universal and particular, hot and non-hot.

stages.heading: What the proof of mental existence must establish
stages.claim: The intended result is not that a material object literally moves into the soul. The claim is that the quiddity or objective content is cognized in a mode of being different from the original thing’s external existence. Al-Ḥillī tests this through cases where the external instance is absent or impossible.
stages.transition: The objection from heat and other material qualities demands a distinction between the object represented and the representing occurrence.

stages.heading: Qūshjī: the form as a psychic quality
stages.claim: Qūshjī locates the cognitive form in the soul and takes its existence in the soul as a psychical quality. This does not erase its object-reference: what is known through it can still be described according to the original quiddity.
stages.transition: The next question is whether the form itself is something externally real, though not externally identical with the thing represented.

stages.heading: Lāhījī: a representation in two different respects
stages.claim: The written word Zayd is the written existence of what it signifies, yet its inked inscription is independently a real external fact. Analogously a scientific form is the mental representation of the known object and itself an actual accident of a real knower. These two predications must not be collapsed.
stages.transition: Once the respects are separated, categorizing the scientific form need not assign all external properties of the signified thing to the soul.

stages.heading: Dawwānī and the dispute over literal categorical quality
stages.claim: Lāhījī explicitly rejects a characterization attributed to Dawwānī in which categorization as a quality is merely figurative. His own assertion that the cognitive form is genuinely a quality is not directly Dawwānī’s position.
stages.transition: This is a real disagreement over the ontology of cognition, not a disagreement about whether one may think of something absent.

stages.heading: Sunni kalām and later commentary as controls
stages.claim: Al-Taftāzānī’s selected passage tests the difference between original external existence and a non-original mental manner of being. Ṭihrānī articulates how the same object can be considered under different modes of existence. They supply comparison, not automatic agreement with Lāhījī.
stages.transition: Only after this distinction is secured may the text argue that the knowing soul is immaterial (Q20); the argument does not follow from mental existence alone.

questions.boundary: Neither this analysis nor the mere formation of an abstract image proves the soul’s immateriality, God’s mode of knowledge, or the independently subsisting reality of universals. Each requires further premises.

questions.title: True predication of absent and negative objects
questions.question: Can true affirmative or negative propositions concern things absent from the external world, and what is the subject of such a proposition?
questions.framing: “The phoenix is imaginary,” “a triangle has three sides,” and “no human is currently on the moon” have different forms of truth. The issue is not solved simply by saying a subject exists mentally: judgments may refer to unrealized but possible instances, impossible combinations, or denials, and their truth-conditions must be identified without treating all their subjects as external objects.

stages.heading: Problem — affirmative judgments without external subjects
stages.claim: We truly predicate relations of impossibilities (for instance, conjunction of contradictories), yet the subjects have no external instances; the form of positive judgment cannot alone establish an external referent.
stages.transition: We need a criterion separating affirming from the existence of the affirmed object.

stages.heading: Two different readings of “establishment”
stages.claim: Lāhījī marks a key distinction: the act of affirmation is not the same as the objective being/obtaining of a putative subject. Merely moving from a true affirmative sentence to an extra-mental thing equivocates. Qūshjī’s three objections, transmitted by Lāhījī, distinguish the coexistence of opposed predicates in a subject from the intellect’s joint conception of existence and its negation.
stages.transition: Formal truth cannot by itself populate the world with impossible objects.

stages.heading: Later direct commentary makes the restriction explicit
stages.claim: A twentieth-century commentator likewise denies that existence-predication presupposes an already existing quiddity. This later voice corroborates the logical distinction, not a medieval textual variant.
stages.transition: The remaining problem is to identify a suitably objective criterion of truth.

Different kinds of absent subject require different treatments; they should not be grouped under an undifferentiated “nonexistent things exist in mind.”

questions.title: Nafs al-amr and objective truth
questions.question: Where does a logically or mathematically correct judgment agree with reality when no corresponding material individual exists?
questions.framing: If “two plus two is four” remains true when no one currently entertains it, what does its correctness correspond to? The term nafs al-amr marks objective correctness without immediately committing its user to a freestanding Platonic world or to a special class of mental entities. One must distinguish the thing as it is, its conceptual presentation, and the relation of correspondence.

stages.heading: The Ṭūsī lemma and initial distinction
stages.claim: The inherited Ṭūsī units introduce correspondence to what is the case in itself; their wording alone does not locate an additional substantial “realm of facts.”
stages.transition: What does correspondence require when no concrete subject exists?

stages.heading: Truth of universally scoped suppositions
stages.claim: A universally quantified judgment can have a logically supposed subject, whose mental supposition need not entail a matching external individual.
stages.transition: But supposing a proposition does not make it true.

stages.heading: Affirmation versus objective obtaining
stages.claim: Lāhījī distinguishes logical assertion from ontological establishment; the two questions must not be conflated.
stages.transition: Now identify the standard of correctness.

stages.heading: Nafs al-amr and grounded relational attributions
stages.claim: Lāhījī states the criterion: the truth of iʿtibārī attributions is correspondence with nafs al-amr, even though the predicate need not itself be a separate extra-mental entity.
stages.transition: This licenses objectivity without reification, but does not settle the ultimate metaphysics of every mathematical or modal truth.

stages.heading: The Ṭihrānī distinction
stages.claim: The inherited exposition separates the meaning of nafs al-amr from the relation of matching it; this confirms that an account of the truth-maker is an additional task. Yazdī objects to identifying nafs al-amr exclusively with the active intellect: divine knowledge has a superior claim as a criterion of reality.
stages.transition: The appeal to divine knowledge in Q24 and fixed entities in Q26 remains a further contested explanation.

stages.claim: Read the following passages in their stated source order. Lāhījī’s alternative interpretations precede his objection; Qūshjī’s reported answer precedes his criticism and decisive reply; İSAM separates Iṣfahānī’s base text from Jurjānī’s gloss. Cross-question placement is editorial comparison, not proof that these authors directly replied to one another.

stages.heading: Continuous witnesses and critical qualifications · second collation
stages.claim: Read the reported position, objection and response in source order. Iṣfahānī’s “new” persistence must be read with Jurjānī’s denial that it is a separately produced external property. Qūshjī’s objection is now available directly. Ghiyāth’s selected ending is catalogue-mediated and its local speaker remains unresolved. Only the records relevant to this debate are linked below.

questions.verdict: The best-supported result is a distinction between having a mental conception and its being objectively correct. Treating nafs al-amr as either nothing but subjective thought or automatically identical to divine knowledge begs the disputed question. The latter relation is a possible later explanation requiring its own sources.
questions.boundary: The inherited materials are inadequate for a complete genealogy of the technical term across al-Ījī, Jurjānī, Mīr Zāhid, and later logicians.
questions.remaining: Second collation has supplied the bounded passages linked above. Collate works directly devoted to nafs al-amr and al-Ījī/Jurjānī/Mīr Zāhid discussions; distinguish mathematical, modal, and divine-science cases. Consult the new critical report for gaps now closed and remaining whole-work and multi-witness work.

questions.title: Modality: necessity, possibility, impossibility
questions.question: Are modal determinations intrinsic, caused, or logical considerations, and how do they apply to nonexistent possibilities?
questions.framing: Necessity, impossibility, and possibility can be considered intrinsically or with reference to another. A contingent existent can be necessary *through its complete cause* without becoming necessary *by its essence*. Confusing these respects either makes contingency vanish when a thing exists or mistakes an intellectual modality for an independently subsisting substance.

stages.heading: Three modalities, and why their cognition is not their being
stages.claim: The possibility, necessity or impossibility of a subject is not simply a further material component that the mind detects alongside it.
stages.transition: Are these three determinations then fictions created by the mind?

stages.heading: Avicennan interpretation defended by Lāhījī
stages.claim: Lāhījī argues that Avicenna’s calling possibility “existent” need mean no more than that the mental attribution has an objective basis from which it is abstracted.
stages.transition: Grounded intellectual considerations differ from freely invented ones.

stages.heading: Nafs al-amr governs the attribution
stages.claim: The criterion of truth for iʿtibārī modal descriptions is their correspondence with nafs al-amr, not an independent extramental property of possibility.
stages.transition: Why does this not violate the principle of contradiction?

stages.heading: Defusing the objection from two nonexistent contradictories
stages.claim: Lāhījī distinguishes whether opposed concepts exist as objects from whether opposite predicates may both be truly applied. Contradiction attaches to the latter, not the former.
stages.transition: Question Q13 turns modal indifference into a dependence argument; additional premises will be required.

stages.heading: 31 October: independently inspected continuation
stages.claim: Read the following passages in their stated source order. Lāhījī’s alternative interpretations precede his objection; Qūshjī’s reported answer precedes his criticism and decisive reply; İSAM separates Iṣfahānī’s base text from Jurjānī’s gloss. Cross-question placement is editorial comparison, not proof that these authors directly replied to one another.

questions.verdict: The modal classification prepares rather than replaces the later causal proofs. In particular, “necessary through another” is not a second instance of the divine intrinsic necessity, and the thesis that a possibility is conceptually predicated does not mean it is arbitrary.
questions.boundary: The full extended post-classical modal analysis remains a primary-source gap; this dossier does not pretend a definition supplied by the matn settles it.
questions.remaining: Retrieve direct extended commentaries at the entire modal block (§§45–76), then compare the relevant Sunni logical treatments.

questions.title: Definition, proof, and explanatory demonstration
questions.question: When is an argument merely inferential (innī), when explanatory (limmī), and what qualifies as a demonstration?
questions.framing: Knowing that something is so is not always the same as knowing why it is so. Demonstration requires conditions on premises, inference and the explanatory middle. This differs from the claim that every valid inference must be a strictly scientific demonstration, and from the claim that direct knowledge by presence is a defective syllogism.

stages.heading: The logical discipline
stages.claim: Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī describes the middle term joining premises and insists on the greater intelligibility of definitions. These are technical rules that help diagnose where the explanatory link sits.
stages.transition: The middle may disclose a cause or only signify it.

stages.heading: A challenge to exclusive reliance on formal definitions
stages.claim: Ibn Taymiyya objects to the premise that a specific apparatus of definition and syllogism is the indispensable route to all knowledge. This is a rival critique of method, not an automatic rejection of rational inference.
stages.transition: The fact of criticism does not determine its correctness.

stages.heading: Ṭihrānī’s analysis of proof type
stages.claim: Ṭihrānī says that a proof of the Necessary can resemble the proof from an effect while also possessing a causal character, without being classifiable as pure burhān al-limm or burhān al-inn in the strict standard.
stages.transition: This complication is relevant at Q23, but the methodological distinction belongs here.

questions.verdict: The dispute is over explanatory force and epistemic privilege, not simply a contest between “reason” and “mysticism.” A correct proof may establish existence without supplying the inner cause; an appeal to unveiling raises a further question of warrant (Q30).
questions.boundary: Neither rejecting a circular definition nor citing insight by presence substitutes for a worked demonstration with identified premises.
questions.remaining: Retrieve relevant Qūshjī, Shīrāzī, al-Rāzī and the post-classical logic commentators with explicit demonstrations and counter-demonstrations.

questions.title: Individuation, unity, and relational categories
questions.question: What individuates a substance, and are unity, plurality, relation and causality real features or second intelligibles?
questions.framing: A father is father only relative to a child; “father” cannot be a free-standing external item unrelated to its correlate. But not every reciprocal relational description entails a separate real accident. Unity likewise may be conceived of actual beings without adding a new independent substance called unity. The issue therefore combines the analysis of categories with the status of relational predicates.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī on unity and relational categories
stages.claim: The matn distinguishes the one and the many and treats many relations and unity as second intelligibles, then places reciprocity among the characteristic properties of relations.
stages.transition: This should not be deduced from an unrelated passage on mental existence.

stages.heading: Unity analysed by al-Ḥillī
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī develops the claim that unity and plurality as predicates are intellectual considerations, using the difficulty of making unity itself a further external entity.
stages.transition: This does not mean that the things counted are fictitious.

stages.heading: Ṭihrānī on reciprocity
stages.claim: Ṭihrānī separates reciprocity in propositions from reciprocity in simple relative terms, and distinguishes strict relation from broader relational naming. The father/son example shows exactly what kind of mutual reference is required.
stages.transition: His distinctions keep the logical exchange of terms from being mistaken for a reciprocal efficient-causal action.

questions.verdict: The core conclusion is categorical, not monistic: relational and numerical descriptions require subjects and correlated respects, but need not be independently subsisting realities. The dependence of relation on termini is different from the relation of an effect to its efficient cause.
questions.boundary: The surviving extracts do not exhaust later disputes on *iḍāfa* as a real accident versus an intellectual relation.
questions.remaining: The present cited excerpts are indirect; obtain direct sharḥ/ḥāshiya sequences for Ṭūsī §§164–179 and Sunnī treatments of relation and unity.

questions.title: Why the contingent needs a cause
questions.question: Is possibility or temporal origination the ground of dependence, and does a contingent being continue to need its cause?
questions.framing: A possible being does not acquire an explanation merely by having once begun. It is contingent because its essence does not entail existence or nonexistence; the fact that it begins at a time is a condition of its existence, not the source of its dependence. This is logically prior to the debate over whether the world begins in time.

stages.heading: Al-Ḥillī’s argument from equal alternatives
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī presents the division between possibility, temporal origination, and both as the ground of need, then argues that the intellect seeks a determining cause when it understands a possible quiddity without first considering its temporal beginning.
stages.transition: This yields an explanatory dependence independent of chronological novelty.

stages.heading: The priority argument
stages.claim: If origination is posterior to existence, and existence posterior to the causal act, origination cannot explain the need which precedes that act in the order of explanation. This is a logical ordering of grounds, not a claim that the cause occurs at an earlier clock-time.
stages.transition: The inference must not illicitly move from ontological priority to perpetual chronological succession.

stages.heading: What the cause actually affects
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī says that the agent does not make blackness *be blackness*, but brings about its existence or nonexistence. The contrast clarifies the difference between explaining essential content and actualisation.
stages.transition: Q14 then asks whether that need persists once the effect already exists.

stages.heading: Boundary: needing a cause is not already a proof of a noncontingent terminus
stages.claim: Dawwānī warns that substituting “needing a noncontingent cause” for “needing another” makes the argument circular. It remains to show why dependence cannot be satisfied by infinitely many mutually conditional contingent stages.
stages.transition: The additional premise is investigated explicitly in Q23 rather than silently assumed in Q13.

stages.heading: Continuous witnesses and critical qualifications · second collation
stages.claim: Read the reported position, objection and response in source order. Iṣfahānī’s “new” persistence must be read with Jurjānī’s denial that it is a separately produced external property. Qūshjī’s objection is now available directly. Ghiyāth’s selected ending is catalogue-mediated and its local speaker remains unresolved. Only the records relevant to this debate are linked below.

questions.verdict: The best-supported position is that the possible needs an efficient cause due to its contingency, not due simply to its onset. One may accept that thesis yet separately argue over eternal creation or temporal creation. The effective cause explains actual existence, not the mere analytic definition of the essence.
questions.boundary: No conclusion about God’s manner of willing or the natural efficacy of intervening agents follows solely from possibility as the ground of need.
questions.remaining: Second collation has supplied the bounded passages linked above. Read the full Rāzian and Sunni cases against the Ḥillī/Tajrīd exchange, and separate dependence of a quiddity from the grant of existence. Consult the new critical report for gaps now closed and remaining whole-work and multi-witness work.

questions.title: Creation, preservation, and divine concurrence
questions.question: Does God’s causal activity remain operative when creatures exist, and what room remains for real secondary causes?
questions.framing: An effect that depends by essence does not cease to be possible after coming into existence. But saying its cause sustains it is not yet a complete theory of how multiple natural causal agents operate together with divine causality. The dossier separates dependence, conservation, mediation, and the much stronger claim of continuous immediate divine action.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī’s persistence lemma: possibility is not extinguished by existence
stages.claim: If possibility explains initial causal need and remains intrinsic to the contingent quiddity, then the contingent remains dependent while it exists. Al-Iṣfahānī’s transmitted lemma anchors this need explicitly to the persistence of possibility.
stages.transition: An objection now asks what further causal action remains to be done after generation.

stages.heading: Al-Ḥillī: the preservation/repetition dilemma
stages.claim: An already actual effect cannot be brought into being again as the same completed event; if the cause produces something newly additional, the objector says it is not preserving the previous effect. The builder analogy appears here, but distinguishes external preparation from principal efficient dependence. Al-Iṣfahānī also formulates the opponent’s dilemma over whether the preserving cause adds a genuine effect.
stages.transition: Al-Ḥillī’s direct reply identifies the new effect not with another object but with its continued existence.

stages.heading: Persistence as a distinct but continuous causal contribution
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī answers that the effect of the cause after origination is preservation, not a second origin; Lāhījī describes this as an uninterrupted flow of existence, not repeated demolition and re-creation. Al-Iṣfahānī frames the new contribution as persistence itself; this remains open to Lāhījī’s later objection about whether the same existence can subsist.
stages.transition: The objection can be sharpened: why cannot an already produced existence itself continue?

stages.heading: Lāhījī’s objection to Jurjānī: heat remains after removal of fire
stages.claim: The conventional light-and-source analogy assumes the kind of dependency under dispute. In his own voice Lāhījī compares heat remaining in warmed water after fire is removed; the persistence of the same result seems compatible with removal of a prior agent.
stages.transition: The reply must distinguish agents that give existence from those that merely dispose the recipient.

stages.heading: Existence-bestowing cause versus preparatory cause
stages.claim: Lāhījī characterizes true existence-giving causation as existential following: the effect is what-it-is through another, not a self-existent remainder. Natural agents in his framework are preparatory.
stages.transition: This develops an ontological claim about dependence, but does not determine exactly which natural agents are true secondary efficient causes.

stages.heading: Metaphysical mediation as a later distinct question
stages.claim: Fanārī’s stronger claim about individual divine-facing dependence and instrumental mediation concerns the distribution of agency among higher and lower causes; it does not follow formally from the bare possibility lemma.
stages.transition: Compare Q15–16 and reserve Akbarī implications for Q27–29.

stages.heading: Continuous witnesses and critical qualifications · second collation
stages.claim: Read the reported position, objection and response in source order. Iṣfahānī’s “new” persistence must be read with Jurjānī’s denial that it is a separately produced external property. Qūshjī’s objection is now available directly. Ghiyāth’s selected ending is catalogue-mediated and its local speaker remains unresolved. Only the records relevant to this debate are linked below.

questions.verdict: There is a genuine shared question across the texts: what explains the effect *now*? But it receives different levels of answer. Contingent existence requires a sustaining ground; whether immediate divine efficacy replaces created efficient causes is an additional thesis, not the logical content of the persistence proof.
questions.boundary: Equating this with Aquinas’s primary/secondary causality is a constructive hypothesis only; the historical intermediary-cause disputes must first be documented.
questions.remaining: Second collation has supplied the bounded passages linked above. Check al-Iṣfahānī §2.66 in print-facsimile, not only searchable snippets; then read the complete Lāhījī/Jurjānī dialectic against its folios before giving a synoptic textual apparatus. Consult the new critical report for gaps now closed and remaining whole-work and multi-witness work.

questions.title: Four causes, complete causes, instruments and conditions
questions.question: How do formal, material, efficient and final causes relate to a complete cause, preparatory conditions, instruments and impediments?
questions.framing: The division into material, formal, efficient and final causes is not four competing answers to the same question. Internal causes explain the effect’s constitution; external causes explain its actual production and the sake for which production occurs. Instruments, conditions, absences of impediments and partial causes raise the challenge of whether the fourfold classification is exhaustive.

stages.heading: Iṣfahānī gives the primary classification
stages.claim: Material cause concerns the effect potentially, formal cause its actuality, efficient cause the source of existence, and final cause the end for whose sake something occurs. Conditions and removal of impediments complete the material or efficient cause.
stages.transition: The examples are explanatory types, not proofs of hylomorphism.

stages.heading: Jurjānī questions the internal-cause division
stages.claim: Jurjānī distinguishes causes of quiddity from causes of existence, then asks about genus and differentia, which are parts of an account of essence but are not straightforwardly material and formal causes.
stages.transition: The objection concerns definitional and physical composition being illegitimately treated as identical.

stages.heading: Qūshjī presses instruments and conditions
stages.claim: Qūshjī questions whether definitions of agent, matter and form properly house instruments, conditions and impediments. These are not merely incidental lists; they challenge which explanans is independently productive.
stages.transition: Al-Ījī’s classification supplies an independent Sunni taxonomy.

stages.heading: Dawwānī tests the composition of a complete cause
stages.claim: In discussing the proof from a totality of contingent beings, Dawwānī separates material and formal constituents from the efficient source and its conditions. This matters because calling the parts of a composite its “complete cause” equivocates between constituent causes and an independent producer. The transfer from individual prior parts to their collection is not automatic.
stages.transition: The question is a genuine causal taxonomy, not merely a verbal objection to proof of the Necessary.

stages.heading: Sunni and direct-text controls
stages.claim: Al-Ījī’s transmitted distinction of productive and final external causes and al-Ḥillī’s concise division of internal/external causes provide controls that do not presuppose Jurjānī’s reply.
stages.transition: Final causes and divine purposiveness are the distinct controversy in Q21.

stages.heading: Continuous witnesses and critical qualifications · second collation
stages.claim: Read the reported position, objection and response in source order. Iṣfahānī’s “new” persistence must be read with Jurjānī’s denial that it is a separately produced external property. Qūshjī’s objection is now available directly. Ghiyāth’s selected ending is catalogue-mediated and its local speaker remains unresolved. Only the records relevant to this debate are linked below.

questions.verdict: The classification must be evaluated according to *what kind of dependence* each cause expresses. The existence of conditions does not require a fifth formal species if they are components of a complete cause; but the assignment is disputed, especially where genus and differentia are confused with material/formal principles.
questions.boundary: This evidence describes causal types but does not show that all natural effects require matter and substantial form; Q17 handles that separate question.
questions.remaining: Second collation has supplied the bounded passages linked above. Translate full al-Iṣfahānī/Qūshjī treatments of conditions and distinguish Ḥillī’s account of the end’s priority in conception and posterior existence. Consult the new critical report for gaps now closed and remaining whole-work and multi-witness work.

questions.title: Real created efficacy and occasionalism
questions.question: Do created natural powers genuinely bring about characteristic effects, or are causal associations only customary sequences?
questions.framing: There are at least three separable theories: corporeal powers act with genuine efficacy, created powers occasion divine effects without producing them, and human voluntary agents act through ordered faculties and bodily instruments. An argument about the latter does not settle the former. This question requires proof at the level of particular natural effects.

stages.heading: The theologians’ immediate-divine-effect thesis
stages.claim: Al-Taftāzānī reports the view that contingent effects come directly from God, so corporeal powers possess no intrinsic efficacy and the spatial conditions insisted upon by philosophers lose their supposed necessity.
stages.transition: This passage records a position within a dispute; it must not be generalized into an undifferentiated Sunni doctrine.

stages.heading: Human voluntary action is a different evidential case
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī’s discussion of our actions distinguishes particular conception, desire, resolve and muscular movement. The causal architecture of voluntary action is not identical with fire heating cotton.
stages.transition: This example shows why the category of “cause” has to be specified rather than assumed to be uniform.

stages.heading: Where the explanations collide
stages.claim: The direct causation thesis questions whether any natural power efficiently produces the result. The voluntary sequence, however, identifies necessary ordered conditions of human action without yet proving independent efficacy. The Qūshjī treatment of instruments in Q15 is the immediate cross-check.
stages.transition: Q14 established the need for conservation; it did not erase this separate created-action problem.

stages.heading: A direct qualification: not every kind of cause bestows existence
stages.claim: Lāhījī explicitly regards the sun, fire and other natural agents as preparatory conditions for forms bestowed by a separate giver. This challenges any too-easy assertion that he and Aquinas defend the same secondary causation.
stages.transition: Whether created agency is genuine as a natural efficient cause is an additional problem; study Q15 and the separate terminology of instrument, cause and preparation.

stages.heading: Continuous witnesses and critical qualifications · second collation
stages.claim: Read the reported position, objection and response in source order. Iṣfahānī’s “new” persistence must be read with Jurjānī’s denial that it is a separately produced external property. Qūshjī’s objection is now available directly. Ghiyāth’s selected ending is catalogue-mediated and its local speaker remains unresolved. Only the records relevant to this debate are linked below.

questions.verdict: The open disagreement is not “God or nature” in a generic sense. It concerns whether God’s action constitutes, conserves, concurs with, or supplants the proximate power that explains a specific change. To resolve it one needs fuller texts from the affirmers and critics of intrinsic natures.
questions.boundary: The existing two witnesses cannot warrant a full historical verdict on occasionalism, the law of custom, and created efficacy across Islamic schools.
questions.remaining: Second collation has supplied the bounded passages linked above. Source substantial opposing passages from al-Ghazālī, al-Rāzī, al-Taftāzānī, Jurjānī, Mullā Ṣadrā and explicit created-action passages in Kashf al-murād. Consult the new critical report for gaps now closed and remaining whole-work and multi-witness work.

questions.title: Substance, body, matter and substantial form
questions.question: What grounds the unity of a material substance, and what follows from continuity, composition and the reality of natural form?
questions.framing: The debate begins with the division of contingent beings into substance and accident, then divides between hylomorphic analyses and alternatives that do not admit prime matter or substantial form as external constituents. A classification of causal factors cannot itself demonstrate matter/form composition; arguments from division, continuity and the existence of atoms must be assessed in their own right.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī’s challenge: division does not prove prime matter
stages.claim: The Tajrīd lemma rules out the claim that divisibility demands a second substrate apart from body. Al-Ḥillī supplies the reductio: matter after division is either newly created (regress if every generation demands matter) or already many (potentially infinitely many actual substrates).
stages.transition: The dilemma works only if the new substrates must each be entirely generated or each preexist as numerically separate actual entities.

stages.heading: An accepted generic notion of material receptivity
stages.claim: Lāhījī carefully distinguishes some substrate persisting through natural transformation from the claim that it is a discrete, nonextended prime substance. The former is accepted across several schools.
stages.transition: The dispute concerns *what* bears transformations, not whether change occurs or has a material bearer.

stages.heading: Rival model: simple extended body
stages.claim: Lāhījī reports a Platonic/Illuminationist account: the extended body itself survives conjunction and separation without an additional hylomorphic constituent.
stages.transition: It is a countermodel to the Peripatetic inference, not a denial of matter in the broad sense.

stages.heading: Peripatetic method of conjunction and separation
stages.claim: The Peripatetics claim the connection/disconnection changes must be evaluated under a substantial notion of continuous body, not just external adjacency or measured dimensions.
stages.transition: If quantitative and intrinsic continuity are confused, the proof equivocates.

stages.heading: The pivot: continuity as numerically one substantial identity
stages.claim: Lāhījī locates the decisive question: does intrinsic substantial continuity constitute numerical identity, and is it destroyed when the body is split?
stages.transition: A satisfactory hylomorphism needs a persistent subject when one continuous substantial form becomes plural.

stages.heading: The continuity-of-material-origin premise
stages.claim: Dividing a jug of water into two vessels is intuitively not a destruction of the whole water and creation of unrelated water ex nihilo. Lāhījī uses that contrast to supply the premise of a remaining element.
stages.transition: Whether this demonstrates *prime matter* rather than more basic physical continuity remains contentious.

stages.heading: Reported Peripatetic conclusion: matter plus corporeal form
stages.claim: The reported argument infers two physical principles: the form of substantial connection is changed, while a non-connected material substrate remains. Lāhījī then records the objection that an absolutely unextended substrate seems incapable of subsequently receiving extension.
stages.transition: Ṭūsī’s infinite-divisibility argument has still to be met; merely presenting the school’s conclusion is insufficient.

stages.heading: Al-Astarābādī’s pointed reply to Ṭūsī
stages.claim: Later al-Astarābādī responds that the matter is one in an undivided continuum and multiple after actual division. No actual infinity of simultaneous distinct substrates is therefore assumed.
stages.transition: But this shifts the burden to explaining how one receptive substrate acquires plurality without generating independent matter from nothing.

stages.heading: Verdict and cross-tradition stakes
stages.claim: One can accept generation, material continuity, and form as intelligible without committing immediately to separate prime matter. The rival parties dispute identity and persistence criteria under division. Thomistic prime matter is a useful comparison only after that distinction is established.
stages.transition: Open issues: direct Avicenna Shifāʾ and al-Rāzī arguments, al-Iṣfahānī and Qūshjī continuous pages, and textual collation against independent print/manuscript witnesses.

questions.verdict: The question is deliberately left substantively contested: which account best explains the unity and transformation of bodies? The present inherited quotations do not contain complete opposing arguments about indivisible atoms, prime matter or substantial form, so the reader states that deficiency. The controlling *Tajrīd* loci are retained below.
questions.boundary: Extended proofs from al-Ḥillī, Qūshjī, Iṣfahānī, *Mawāqif* and philosophical natural science have not yet been translated as a coherent pair of opposing cases.
questions.remaining: Substantial gaps: extract long atomism/continuity arguments from Ḥillī, Qūshjī and Mawāqif; compare Shīrāzī and Ṣadrā on substantial form.

questions.title: Potency, actuality, and the continuity of motion
questions.question: What is a subject of change, and is a motion a real successive actualization or an abstraction across temporal stages?
questions.framing: The concept of motion is not the mere enumeration of successive positions: an account of a continuously changing body must explain the subject, the ordered boundary positions and the aspect under which change is actual. Motion as existing in the changing thing is also distinct from a composite representation constituted in imagination.

stages.heading: The foundational choice of a definition
stages.claim: Ṭūsī presents motion both as the first actuality of a potential subject precisely as potential and as successive occupation of places; al-Ḥillī makes clear these are philosophical and kalām conceptions respectively.
stages.transition: The philosophical account implies a subject still capable of further determination while its motion occurs.

stages.heading: Terms required for a real motion
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī enumerates six terms: initial and terminal states, efficient and receptive principles, the domain of movement, and temporal duration. Without such distinctions, motion collapses into an unanalysed series of events.
stages.transition: But not every ontological category can be a changing determination.

stages.heading: Why substantial motion is excluded in the received account
stages.claim: For al-Ḥillī, the accepted categories of motion are quantity, quality, place and position; a simple substance comes into existence all at once. Thus “motion in substance” requires changing a substantial premise, not mere terminological accommodation.
stages.transition: The identity of what persists through motion is the relevant metaphysical constraint.

stages.heading: Lāhījī’s substrate test
stages.claim: Lāhījī requires that the mover remain a constituted existent without the particular changing determination. This is why motion in quiddity’s own existence is especially problematic.
stages.transition: Can successive existences nevertheless constitute one enduring individual?

stages.heading: Objection against succession of existences
stages.claim: Lāhījī argues that, if successive existence-instances are potential during motion, the moving essence never has the actual existence required to be a mover. The reply requires an account of identity across ontological renewal, not just the image of intensifying heat.
stages.transition: Ṣadrā’s account of substantial motion directly contests this inherited criterion; this sourcebook must not attribute Ṣadrian doctrine to Ṭūsī or Lāhījī.

stages.heading: Earlier inherited motion discussion
stages.claim: Ṭihrānī’s observation that motion is established by experience can supplement but cannot replace the above causal and substrate analysis.
stages.transition: Compare Q17 on matter’s identity and Q20 on the soul’s development.

questions.verdict: The lesson is to distinguish the metaphysics of an undergoing subject, the temporal structure of change and the intellect’s or imagination’s synthetic representation. The inherited evidence is strong for the distinction but not yet for a complete theory of intrinsic potency and act.
questions.boundary: The title “continuity of motion” cannot substitute for the missing proofs of continuity, potentiality, and the contrary theories of motion.
questions.remaining: Collate Ṭūsī’s underlying physical passages and commentators, then include Ibn Sīnā’s motion and Ṣadrā’s substantial motion as parallel rather than direct Tajrīd glosses.

questions.title: Origination, eternity, and causal necessity
questions.question: Does metaphysical contingency entail a temporal beginning, and how do substantial generation and perpetual preservation interact?
questions.framing: A world may be argued to be contingent in existence without that argument already proving that it began at some finite past time. Conversely, a proof of temporal origination may depend on a theory of atoms, accidents, free choice or temporal succession. The present question therefore separates the mode of being caused from the chronology of a caused world.

stages.heading: The beginning/necessity distinction
stages.claim: The argument of Q13 makes contingency the reason for needing a cause. It cannot be turned directly into a demonstration of temporal beginning. Temporal origination appears at another explanatory level.
stages.transition: The distinction blocks an invalid shortcut both for philosophical eternalists and for proponents of temporal creation.

stages.heading: Al-Taftāzānī’s objection to a necessitarian premise
stages.claim: Al-Taftāzānī rejects an argument that presupposes an eternal Maker must produce by necessity of nature. A voluntary agent can bring about a temporal effect when willing it.
stages.transition: This is a criticism of a premise, not a complete proof that time itself began.

stages.heading: Necessity and agency are not identical alternatives
stages.claim: Lāhījī reports that philosophers posit divine agency unlike both animal deliberation and compelled corporeal motion. This is a report embedded in criticism, not a proof that necessary emanation and voluntary choice are compatible.
stages.transition: The remaining debate must therefore specify the sense of choice, the modality of the effect, and the distinction between causal necessity and compulsion.

stages.heading: A direct comparative kalām argument
stages.claim: Al-Miqdād al-Siyūrī, in an independent kalām text rather than a *Tajrīd* commentary, reasons from the continual dependence of bodies on originated accidents to the world’s origination.
stages.transition: The further premise, that whatever cannot be free of originated events must itself be originated, needs independent scrutiny.

stages.heading: Lāhījī qualifies ancient possible beings and voluntary divine action
stages.claim: In expounding Ṭūsī’s distinction between a necessary sufficient antecedent and an agent intending an as-yet unproduced effect, Lāhījī distinguishes extra-essential intention from intrinsic divine willing. A philosopher may deny qasd in the first sense while affirming ikhtiyār in another.
stages.transition: This is evidence for a historical terminological dispute; it is not the same as adjudicating eternity, creation or free will between Ibn Sīnā and Aquinas.

questions.verdict: These positions confront different explanatory models, not merely different dates for creation. The exact transition from “body necessarily bears accidents” to “body begins” is disputed; so is the transition from the causal sufficiency of a complete cause to the eternality of its effect. A proper debate needs both arguments displayed without making either a caricature.
questions.boundary: Neither the sole short Sunni quotation nor the corpus excerpt is the complete historically layered eternity controversy. It is marked open rather than filled with Q13 repetitions.
questions.remaining: Retrieve Ḥillī, al-Ījī, al-Taftāzānī, Qūshjī and al-Lāhījī on the beginning of the world and eternal dependence.

questions.title: Soul, faculties, imagination, and acquired perfection
questions.question: Which cognitional operations belong to the soul, to an organ, or to an instrument, and can repeated activity perfect an intrinsic capacity?
questions.framing: The soul’s definition as first perfection is not equivalent to declaring it a material form in the body. Its faculties include sensation, representation, intellect, desire and volition; these can operate through bodily instruments, while intellectual understanding invites a further claim about immateriality. A *malaka* is an acquired capacity, not the momentary occurrence of one cognitive act.

stages.heading: The soul as a first perfection of an organic body
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī begins from the standard account of the soul as the first perfection of an organic natural body. A definition of soul through its operation on a body is not yet a proof of its immateriality.
stages.transition: One must distinguish the soul’s relation to bodily organs from its identity with the undergoing changes of those organs.

stages.heading: Bodily replacement and personal continuity
stages.claim: The identity across replacement argument contrasts continual bodily decay and renewal with the continued identity of the subject. Whether the argument establishes a subsisting soul, and not merely relative psychological continuity, requires scrutiny.
stages.transition: Al-Ḥillī moves from the body’s mutability to the status of the persistent knower; later commentators give the metaphysical categories more sharply.

stages.heading: Lāhījī: independence of matter in essence
stages.claim: In his discussion of the rational soul, Lāhījī construes its substantiality through non-inherence in matter. He reports this as following from immateriality, not as an independent proof of it.
stages.transition: This avoids the circular inference that the soul must be immaterial simply because it is called a substance.

stages.heading: Al-Astarābādī: immaterial in itself, bodily instruments in operation
stages.claim: Al-Astarābādī explicitly distinguishes the soul from a separate intellect: the rational soul does not inhere in matter as a substance, yet requires bodily instruments for some actions. This reconciles the soul’s substantial independence with physiological dependence.
stages.transition: A further question now becomes how powers acquired through those instruments perfect the enduring intellectual subject.

stages.heading: Acquired disposition and cognition
stages.claim: Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī distinguishes acquired dispositional power from actual knowledge. The Māwāqif discussion of reflexive awareness belongs to a separate question concerning consciousness of consciousness: it is recorded as a comparison, not used as proof for the previous conclusion.
stages.transition: The next cross-reference is Q24: divine knowing cannot be modeled as acquisition of a disposition by an initially unknowing subject.

questions.verdict: The dossier establishes a historically articulated distinction between a soul’s dependence on bodily organs in exercise and its putative independence of matter in essence; it also distinguishes powers or dispositions from acts of knowing.
questions.boundary: The selected texts do not complete all the medieval demonstrations of immateriality, the question of postmortem individuation, or a full theory of imagination; these must not be declared settled.
questions.remaining: Retrieve full Tajrīd soul chapter and al-Iṣfahānī, Qūshjī, Shīrāzī and the Sunni psychological debates, including immediate knowledge of self.

questions.title: Final causality, providence, and the good
questions.question: Can ends account for natural operations and divine providence without making God act to obtain something He lacks?
questions.framing: Final causes can explain why a maker acts or why a natural process occurs, but the end may be conceptually prior to an act while becoming actual only afterward. Applied to God this structure becomes controversial: if a divine act serves a purpose, does God acquire some perfection from it, or can there be wisdom and benefit without need?

stages.heading: The efficient/final order
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī explains how the envisaged end moves the agent before the action while the achieved end follows it in existence. This distinguishes priority in explanation from priority in time.
stages.transition: Without the distinction, final causes appear self-contradictory.

stages.heading: A shared causal classification
stages.claim: The explanatory tradition surrounding the *Mawāqif* agrees that the final cause is “for whose sake” a thing is produced and that it is produced as a result in external order. The explicit source is indexed under Q15.
stages.transition: The real dispute here is its application to divine action.

stages.heading: Sunni objections and qualification
stages.claim: Al-Jurjānī and attached gloss material deny purposes that perfect the divine agent while allowing innumerable wisdoms and benefits in the outcomes. Both halves of the reported qualification must be read together.
stages.transition: It is not accurate to translate this into “divine action is purposeless” in an unqualified sense.

questions.verdict: The dispute is over the precise meaning of an end as an explanatory cause. Human builders act to gain goods; divine action cannot be explained by God’s deficient state seeking completion. Whether real finality belongs to created natures and divine providence remains a further substantive question.
questions.boundary: Aquinas’s account of God as the end of creatures is a useful later comparison, not a substitute for the full kalām objections and their internal replies.
questions.remaining: Collate original later glosses within Sharḥ al-Mawāqif, Qūshjī, and Lāhījī; add direct Sunni accounts of divine purpose.

questions.title: Divine simplicity, emanation, and the one-from-one rule
questions.question: Can an absolutely simple First explain multiple differentiated effects, and what is the force of relational or conceptual multiplicity?
questions.framing: The “one from one” principle is easily misstated as “anything causes only one thing.” The philosopher’s stronger formulation concerns what proceeds from an utterly simple cause insofar as it is one, without other conditions or differentiating respects. Critics ask whether these qualifications rescue the proof or presuppose the conclusion; and whether a freely choosing agent falls under it at all.

stages.heading: The initial direct commentary
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī connects Ṭūsī’s statement about the one cause to the First Intellect and the explanation of derivative multiplicity through relations. What counts as a sufficient differentiating respect remains the question.
stages.transition: The principle is located in an emanationist metaphysics, not generic causal arithmetic.

stages.heading: Simplicity is not yet the one-from-one rule
stages.claim: Lāhījī excludes intellectual parts from the Necessary on the premise that divine existence and quiddity are identical. A further argument is needed to show that this simplicity restricts direct emanation to a single first effect.
stages.transition: Now assess the one-from-one demonstration and its objections without treating divine noncomposition as a sufficient proof.

stages.heading: Qūshjī reconstructs and contests the inference
stages.claim: Qūshjī isolates the absolute-unity hypothesis, notes the exception claimed for a voluntary agent with multiple acts of willing, reproduces an argument from differing respects of sourcehood, and turns that argument against its own concept of sourcehood.
stages.transition: The disagreement is about the proof, its scope, and what counts as an independent source of differentiation.

stages.heading: Lāhījī qualifies the principle
stages.claim: Lāhījī insists on unity from every respect and discusses whether freedom or necessity, as differently construed, changes the conclusion. His defence is neither a trivial proposition nor a demonstration of the entire Neoplatonic sequence.
stages.transition: Its compatibility with divine freedom remains disputed.

stages.heading: The Qūnawī–Ṭūsī exchange
stages.claim: Qūnawī challenges how relational multiplicity could explain real differentiation without partitioning the First and considers one effused existence with numerous determinations. Ṭūsī answers that conceptual and negative considerations can differentiate explanatory respects without multiplying the First Essence.
stages.transition: One must assess whether conceptual distinctions can bear the requested causal weight.

questions.verdict: There are two principal opposed strategies: real differentiating principles in secondary effects and intellectually distinguished respects grounded in the source or its relation to what proceeds. Qūnawī’s alternative shifts what counts as the “one” first effect. A coherent reading cannot infer either the universal First Intellect scheme or a doctrine of one diffused existence from the short rule alone.
questions.boundary: The full Dawwānī–Dashtakī response chain is still missing. A late editor’s Akbarī note attached to al-Ḥillī must not be mislabelled as al-Ḥillī’s own position.
questions.remaining: Map every objection/reply of the direct commentaries, the Qūnawī correspondence, and Shīrāzī’s doctrines of causation and multiplicity.

questions.title: The Necessary: existence, essence and proof
questions.question: Does the dependence of all contingent things entail a Necessary Existent, and can the proof avoid treating a group as a separate caused object?
questions.framing: Ṭūsī offers several anti-regress arguments. Al-Ḥillī questions the initial proof and separately reconstructs an argument from the totality. Dawwānī presents and tests the latter in detail, records al-Kātibī’s objections, and tries to establish the necessity of an unconditioned ground without circularity. These are distinct arguments and must not be merged.

stages.heading: Ṭūsī: several distinct proofs, not one
stages.claim: The initial proof from necessary causes and the totality argument are distinct Tajrīd lemmata (210 and 213). The former reasons that a chain of beings necessary through others needs an intrinsically necessary cause; the latter tests whether all causes of a totality could lie among its parts. Lemma 572 applies the anti-regress conclusion to proving a Maker.
stages.transition: Before accepting either proof, ask whether the premise is independent of the conclusion.

stages.heading: Al-Ḥillī: a reservation and a separate totality proof
stages.claim: Al-Ḥillī records a reservation concerning the first proof, then sets out the totality proof: the collective is contingent, cannot cause itself, and supposedly cannot be caused by a member. His statement that the totality is possible because its members are possible is precisely the premise later scrutinized.
stages.transition: The objector can challenge the independent causal standing of the collective.

stages.heading: The totality is not automatically another object
stages.claim: Dawwānī clarifies whether one speaks of existing members or an extra imagined collective arrangement. One candidate analysis treats the “totality” merely as several effects considered together; its explanation might then be several causes, without the further demand for a numerically single cause of the group.
stages.transition: A demonstrative proof must show that a relevant totality has a cause without reifying an act of counting.

stages.heading: Complete cause versus its material, formal, and efficient components
stages.claim: Dawwānī reconstructs an opponent’s use of a complete efficient cause but warns that definitions of completeness and the role of constituents matter. The proof’s decisive point is ruling out a cause that is one of the collection’s parts.
stages.transition: The proof now concentrates on the disputed “part” alternative, rather than assuming it eliminated.

stages.heading: Al-Kātibī’s objection and Dawwānī’s critique
stages.claim: Dawwānī reports al-Kātibī’s explicit challenge to the claim that the totality is caused by all its members. He then rejects the transfer from each part’s priority to the priority of all parts together; a group cannot become an efficient cause simply because each constituent bears some causal relation.
stages.transition: Thus, at least one version of the collective proof fails unless its central mereological premise is supplied.

stages.heading: A distinct route: necessity through another is conditional
stages.claim: A causally sufficient thing may itself be caused, so sufficiency for an effect does not entail intrinsic necessity. Dawwānī instead treats necessity-through-another as a conditional: if the antecedent cause is posited, the consequent is required. Infinitely many such conditionals do not, merely by their number, posit an existing unconditioned antecedent.
stages.transition: This supplies a fresh argument for why an actual contingent order calls for an unconditioned actuality, although its full formal validity remains to be tested.

stages.heading: The final anti-circularity check
stages.claim: Dawwānī challenges an argument that effectively defines dependence as dependence on the noncontingent. That already assumes the conclusion. The project must distinguish need, sufficiency, necessity-through-another, the actuality of the series, and intrinsic necessity.
stages.transition: Only now do the broader comparison with al-Rāzī, Taftāzānī, and Aquinas, and the ontological question of manifestation (Q27), become meaningful.

stages.heading: Separate theological and mystical extensions
stages.claim: Ṭūsī’s divine-existence lemma, the direct Qūnawī–Ṭūsī exchange, and Jāmī’s later argument need to be read after the demonstrations. The existence of a first cause alone does not establish identity of created and divine being or an Akbarī account of manifestation.
stages.transition: See Q26–29 for fixed entities and unity, and Q14–15 for dependence and causal taxonomy.

stages.heading: 31 October: independently inspected continuation
stages.claim: Read the following passages in their stated source order. Lāhījī’s alternative interpretations precede his objection; Qūshjī’s reported answer precedes his criticism and decisive reply; İSAM separates Iṣfahānī’s base text from Jurjānī’s gloss. Cross-question placement is editorial comparison, not proof that these authors directly replied to one another.

questions.verdict: The whole/parts proof is historically contested and its “cause of the totality” premise must not be smuggled in. The conditional-necessity strategy avoids some mereological pitfalls, but a complete demonstration still owes the link between actually existing dependent beings and a noncontingent existential ground.
questions.boundary: One must not infer the impossibility of all infinite structures from a restriction argued only for a per se dependent causal series; nor infer Akbarī numerical unity of existence from the existence of a Necessary First Cause.
questions.remaining: Lāhījī’s formerly missing electronic pp.470–472 are recovered and translated within the complete Ishāra main text (scan printed pp.462–466).
